entries.title: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
entries.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election

November 28, 2026

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday hit the campaign trail one last time before Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, telling people to "vote, vote, vote" to make sure the country doesn't go "backwards."

Opinion polls point to a change in government, with the conservative People's Party (PP) slated to come out on top, bringing an end to Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership.

Spain's general election this Sunday is also crucial because it kicks off a round of elections on the continentand because it is yet another test of the region's shift to the right.  

The PP would potentially have to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form the next government in Spain.

There's also a chance that the election ends in a hung parliament, with neither the right-wing coalition nor the left bloc securing a majority.

Sanchez has so far campaigned on a platform of having boosted the Spanish economy when its European Union partners were struggling.

He has pointed to his policies of having increased the minimum wage and having lifted pensions in line with inflation.

But people are frustrated that the cost of living has soared and that they're not able to enjoy the fruits of economic growth, with many unable to leave their parents' house because of very high rental prices.

Sanchez doubles down on attempt to appeal to leftist voters

Sanchez said during his final rally in Madrid that the "elections are about moving Spain forward, not moving it backwards."

He doubled down on an attempt to appeal to left-leaning voters, telling them that a right coalition government, with far-right members in parliament, would reverse the years of social progress and gut public services.

Oscar-winning Spanish film director Pedro Almodovar was also at the rally this evening.

Sanchez wore a red T-shirt that said "the power of the people," telling people that a "progressive majority is within our reach."

Sanchez has also become the standard-bearer for Europeans frustrated with the Trump administration.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo dismisses Sanchez's campaign of 'fear'

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has said that he wants to maintain good relations with US President Donald Trump, dismissed Sanchez's campaign of "fear."

Feijoo won the most seats during elections in 2023, but he was not able to form a government.

"And when a government has nothing to offer but fear, it means it has nothing else left to offer," he told supporters at his campaign finale in the southern city of Seville.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," said Feijoo, who built his career running central public bodies and the northwestern Galicia region.

He has advocated for tough immigration policies and stronger border management.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, favors a much tougher approach, with his party having advocated for mass deportations.

Addressing a closing rally at a bullring in the eastern city of Valencia, Abascal told supporters not to "vote out of fear. Vote with courage."

"What we are up against is a criminal mafia led by a ruthless boss, a liar," he said, referring to the corruption scandals that have surrounded Sanchez and his government.

entries.title: US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade
entries.summary: The United States said it was continuing "to strictly enforce the blockade" of Iran's ports. Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over a strike that killed two Italian technicians.
entries.content:
Iran

US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade

November 28, 2026

The United States said it was continuing "to strictly enforce the blockade" of Iran's ports. Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over a strike that killed two Italian technicians.

The United States military on Friday announced it had fired at a ship in the Gulf of Oman that it said was violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports.

A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" in the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer, US Central Command (CENTCOM), said, adding that it "continues to strictly enforce the [US] blockade."

CENTCOM oversees US forces in the Middle East.

The statement said that "the ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled" and stressed that "the civilian crew was unharmed."

It said that the ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas.

The US blockade has disabled six ships and redirected 158 others.

Washington launched its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July following the collapse of an agreement with Tehran.

The war broke out in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which prompted Tehran to impose its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over strike on military site

Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a Thursday drone strike killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti military site.

A Kuwaiti citizen and a Pakistani citizen were also injured and hospitalized in the attack.

Iran has denied responsibility for the strike.

Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Al-Mashaan condemned the "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defense.

The two technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, a subsidiary of the German defense firm Rheinmetall.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, calling on "all parties to exercise restraint."

Guterres is "deeply concerned by the continued escalation in the region," according to his spokesman, Stephane Dujarric. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

entries.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
entries.summary: Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill

November 27, 2026

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

entries.title: Germany news: Lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
entries.summary: German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Parliament approves €556 billion 2027 budget

Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026

German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates have been closed.

Below, you can review DW's coverage of what Germany was talking about on Friday, 27 November. 

  • German lawmakers approve 2027 federal budget
  • Left Party hosts summit on femicide and violence against women
  • BSW party conference starts in Dresden
  • Rheinmetall lowers revenue forecasts
  • Chancellor Merz to meet Pope Leo on Monday

Skip next section Chequered skipper wins Germany's 2027 butterfly of the year award

Chequered skipper wins Germany's 2027 butterfly of the year award

The checkered or arctic skipper, carterocephalus palaemon, has been named the 2027 butterfly of the year by BUND, the German Federation for the Environment and Nature Conservation.

As so often, the animal has a more literal and descriptive moniker in German, where it's known as the gelbwürfelige Dickkopffalter, or "yellow-checked thick-headed butterfly" — an homage to two of its most distinguishing features, its coloration and its large head.

BUND said that with its choice for 2027 it wanted to "raise awareness about the loss of valuable water-based ecosystems." It said that the loss of transitional areas between woods and open land with long grasses were crucial to both the butterfly and the caterpillars and were being lost.

"Forest and path edges are often mowed short. With this, the butterflies' feeding and wintering locations are lost. The climate crisis is also weighing on the checkered skipper: for the caterpillars' development, carterocephalus palaemon needs damp living spaces or at least a damp microclimate."

The species is not classified as endangered in Germany at present, but its numbers are in decline.

Skip next section Synagogue attack suspect had been on German deportation list, but was then granted a reprieve

Synagogue attack suspect had been on German deportation list, but was then granted a reprieve

One of the two Iraqi nationals arrested yesterday on suspicion of plotting an attack on Cologne synagogue had been placed on a list of people who should leave the country in 2024, according to North Rhine-Westphalia's Refugee Ministry. 

The 34-year-old Ameer J. appears to have been placed on a list of people from Iraq who were nominally supposed to leave the country but who were granted a dispensation to stay known in German as a "Duldung," stemming from the word for tolerate.

"The first information available to us indicates that one of the two suspects was included on the so-called Unna List that our ministry compiled in the autumn of 2024," NRW's Refugee Minister Verena Schäfer told regional broadcaster WDR.

This followed similar reporting in German media, including from the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper and Der Spiegel.

WDR cited authorities in the city of Cologne as saying the decision to tolerate the man staying was based on him having regular employment at the time, and because he was not in need of replacement passport documentation given his valid Iraqi passport.

The regional broadcaster also reported, citing security sources, that the alleged Islamist had been under observation for several months, partly after he was noticed by investigators looking into an attack on a Jewish site in Munich in April of 2026.

The two men arrested on Thrusday were accused of plotting attacks against the synagogue in Cologne and one other, unnamed, European city. They are thought to have been working for or in conjunction with a pro-Iranian terrorist group. Prosecutors said that, for reasons that were not yet clear, the planned attacks were not ultimately carried out.

Skip next section France's Melenchon visits Berlin to plug book, meet Left Party

France's Melenchon visits Berlin to plug book, meet Left Party

French hard-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon visited Berlin on Friday, and said he sees "a need for a thorough overhaul of the Franco-German relationship."

Melenchon, who is hoping the radical economic platform he's championed for decades in France might finally resonate with voters in the vacuum left by Emmanuel Macron as he hits term limit in April's presidential elections, said he opposed the German government's spending and defense policies. 

"I am hostile to the liberal [economic] policy of German governments that dominates the European Union," the 75-year-old said.

Melenchon advocates drastically increasing public spending in France, already the much more debt-laden of the EU's top two economies, and canceling French debt held by the European Central Bank in order to do so — a step that critics argue would risk damaging both France and Europe's economies more generally.

The 75-year-old said he also rejected Chancellor Friedrich Merz's plan to increase German defense spending.

"We have the duty to ask: to make war against whom," Melenchon said, warning that a stronger Germany could make nuclear-armed France and the rest of Europe a "target" for other countries.

"They need to tone it down, because this one-upmanship leads nowhere," he said.

Melenchon has enshrined leaving NATO and nationalizing defense companies in his party's election platform, prompting allegations of him cosying up to Russian President Vladimir Putin. 

He rejected the notion that he was "Germanophobic," citing his political or musical affection for Karl Marx and Beethoven.

He touted his party's ties with Germany's Left Party (die Linke) and met with party chair Ines Schwerdtner in the capital on Friday while plugging the German translation of his book. 

The Left, too, has criticized Germany's defense spending plans. It's increasingly vague on the question of NATO, no longer explicitly calling for an immediate exit as it once did, but still advocating "replacing" NATO with some other kind of collective European security architecture.

Skip next section Germans in favor of continued European military support for Ukraine — survey

Germans in favor of continued European military support for Ukraine — survey

European military backing for Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion continues to enjoy widespread support in Germany, according to the results of a new survey published on Friday.

The representative "Politbarometer" poll published by public broadcaster ZDF found that 37% of Germans consider the current level of European support for Ukraine to be just right, while another 31% think it should be increased. Fewer than 30% were in favor of a reduction in military support.

The survey also found that almost two thirds of Germans (64%) think Russia poses a large (39%) or very large (25%) threat to Germany, while the rest consider the threat posed by Moscow to be not so big (23%) or non-existent (11%).

When broken down politically, the survey found that supporters of almost all parties consider the danger posed by Russia to be big or very big. Only far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voters bucked the trend with 75% believing that Moscow poses either no threat at all or only a minor one.

The ZDF survey results differ slightly from those published by the Körber foundation on Tuesday, which suggested for the first time that German military backing for Ukraine no longer enjoyed majority support among the population.

The ZDF survey, however, asked respondents about "European" support for Ukraine rather than about Germany specifically.

Skip next section Former German spy chief loses detention appeal

Former German spy chief loses detention appeal

A former German spy chief who is accused of acquiring confidential information supplied to him by a former bureau chief has lost his appeal against pre-trial detention.

August Hanning, the former head of Germany's federal intelligence service (Bundesnachrichtendienst or BND) from 1998-2005, was arrested in October on suspicion of purchased highly sensitive documents from his former colleague and using them as part of intelligence analyses in his role as a private consultant.

Hanning is suspected of having prepared one such analysis for Azerbaijan's domestic intelligence service, although it's unclear whether or not classified information ever actually reached Baku.

At the start of November, Hanning's lawyer appealed against what he called a "disproportionate" pre-trial detention, telling Der Spiegel news magazine that his client had not given away any state secrets nor had the intention of doing so. He also told the dpa news agency that Hanning, 80, did not pose a flight risk.

However, the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof or BGH) has rejected the appeal.

Skip next section German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans

German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans

German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63."

At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.

In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.

From 2029 onwards, however, only periods of employment, child-rearing, and the care of relatives will count toward the 45-year contribution requirement.

Periods during which an insured person received unemployment benefits, sickness benefits or transitional allowances – or held only a low-wage, part-time "mini-job" – will no longer be credited.

For weeks, Germany's coalition government partners, the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and Schweitzer's center-left Social Democrats have been struggling to reach a compromise on this issue.

A pension commission had proposed abolishing this popular type of pension, a proposal opposed by the SPD.

A group of leading coalition politicians, including Schweitzer, reportedly held final discussions regarding the plans as recently as Wednesday evening.

Skip next section German parliament approves 2027 budget

German parliament approves 2027 budget

Germany's ‌lower ⁠house ⁠of parliament, the Bundestag, ​voted in favor of ​a €556 ​billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost ​defense ​and infrastructure spending.

Total new borrowing will reach €210 ​billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in ​2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild ​its military after decades of underinvestment.

"It is right that we invest in the railways and ​in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday, defending his budget. "It is right... that we invest in our security."

German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.

"We are putting up the ⁠money for ​defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil said. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again."

But there was criticism of the budget from the opposition Left Party, with party leader Ines Schwerdtner accusing the government only ever talking about emergency and war.

"But for millions of people in this country, the emergency comes every month when money gets tight," she said. "But you're not interested in these emergencies."

317 members of parliament voted in favor of the budget and 260 against it. There were no abstentions.

Skip next section Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo

Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will have a private audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Monday before meeting Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome later, a government spokesman confirmed on Friday.

Merz, himself a Catholic, had a brief encounter with Pope Leo at the pontiff's inauguration in May 2025, but this will be the pair's first private meeting.

According to Politico, who first reported on the planned meeting earlier this week, officials expect the discussion to focus on "human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine."

Afterwards, Merz will be received with military honors by Italian Prime Minister Meloni, with whom he will hold talks on Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, economic cooperation and, "with certainty," the European Union budget for the period 2028-2034, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF).

Negotiations over the MFF in Brussels this week ended without agreement, with Germany leading a group of more fiscally conservative member states which also includes Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Italy, on the other hand, along with countries like Poland and Spain, would like to see a more ambitious EU budget.

Skip next section Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast

Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast

German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has revised its medium-term revenue forecast for 2030 down from around €45 billion to between €33 billion and €37 billion, with an expected profit margin of around 20%.

The announcement, made on Friday at a market event in Hamburg, comes after the Düsseldorf-based company also lowered its forecast for the current year following delays in major orders  notably from the German government.

In July, the German defense ministry canceled a multi-billion-euro contract to produce six new type-F126 naval frigates and there are now reportedly delays in an expected large-scale order of Boxer armored fighting vehicles (AFV).

Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger said the government was negotiating hard on price and that he would only sign off on the deal once "sufficient profitability" was guaranteed.

Meanwhile, Rheinmetall is set to deliver 66 additional Lynx AFVs to Romania, part of an order which now totals 298 such vehicles.

The deliveries to the European Union and NATO member state are set to begin in 2028 and be completed by 2030.

Rheinmetall is also manufacturing four battleships for the Romanian navy and has increased its production capacities in the eastern European country which borders Ukraine.

Skip next section Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack

Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack

German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has confirmed that two of its employees had been killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.

"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, providing technical support for air-defense systems," the Düsseldorf-based company said in a statement.

"Protecting the people of that country was a matter of deep personal importance to them. Both the company's leadership and the entire workforce are devastated by the loss of our colleagues. We share in the grief of those they have left behind."

The two victims were Italian citizens who worked as technicians for subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirmed in Rome.

Tajani said the pair had been at an air surveillance station in Kuwait when it was attacked by two Iranian drones. Two other people, a Pakistani national and Kuwaiti army captain, were also injured.

The Iranian foreign ministry has denied any involvement in the deadly attack.

Rheinmetall secured a contract to supply the Kuwaiti navy with defense systems in July.

Skip next section BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference

BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference

Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.

The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.

After initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

BSW split over stance on AfD

Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — with which it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.

Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain issues which an AfD minority government would want to implement.

The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.

The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy."

"We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but said: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media."

Wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority."

But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.

"Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term."

They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier."

Skip next section Left Party hosts international femicide summit

Left Party hosts international femicide summit

Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is on Friday hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

Under the title "Voices Against Femicide," the summit in Berlin brings together activists, politicians and researchers from around the world, including Kenya, Nigeria, Kurdistan, India, Afghanistan, Syria, Mexico, Argentina, Spain and Germany.

Across three panel discussions, the speakers will highlight women's rights, feminist struggles and legal perspectives and debate political measures which are urgently needed in Germany to effectively combat femicides and patriarchal violence.

The summit comes just two days after Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, marked Orange Day, the United Nations' officially named day for the elimination of violence against women, with a minute's silence and a series of speeches.

Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office reported a total of 1,176 female victims of attempted and completed homicide in 2025, up from 859 in 2024.

The number of female victims of domestic violence in Germany in 2025 rose by 2.8% to 197,667.

Skip next section German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027

German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027

German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.

The plans call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germanyis talking about on Friday, 27 November.

The German parliament, the Bundestag, is set to vote on a 2027 federal budget that foresees around €556 billion ($610 billion) in spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

Also in Berlin, Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

Meanwhile, the left-wing populist BSW party is holding its party convention in Dresden as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats.

entries.title: Spanish rider Marc Marquez announces MotoGP retirement, days after clinching record 8th world title
entries.summary: Marc Marquez took fans and his team by surprise when announcing this weekend's race in Valencia will be his last. The 33-year-old won a record eight MotoGP titles, including his rookie and retirement seasons.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

Marc Marquez took fans and his team by surprise when announcing this weekend's race in Valencia will be his last. The 33-year-old won a record eight MotoGP titles, including his rookie and retirement seasons.

Marc Marquez, one of the most successful motorcycle racers of all time, announced on Friday that he would retire from MotoGP world championship after this weekend's season finale in Valencia.

The 33-year-old Spaniard's decision comes just a few days after he clinched his eighth top-tier motorcycle racing championship, equaling the record of Italian great Giacomo Agostini set in 1975 and surpassing the seven career titles of Marquez's own childhood hero and later rival Valentino Rossi.  

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage and shown during Friday's free practice.

He did not issue any firm comments about what he planned next, saying: "I first need to understand what I need in my next life."

Why did Marquez say he was retiring now?

The move came as a surprise, not least given that earlier this year Marquez had signed a contract extension with his Ducati team that was set to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old, who has battled with repeated injuries and surgeries in the latter half of his career, said he made the decision after last month's Japanese Grand Prix in light of the physical and mental toll of his battles for fitness.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," he said. "When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder [in May]."

Marquez said that at times this season, chasing a massive deficit after his early-season injury to come back and win the championship, he had begun to "feel the fear" in the saddle, and even noticed brief recurrences of the double vision he struggled with a few years ago.

"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he said.

Who is Marc Marquez?

Marquez burst onto the scene in MotoGP in 2013, highly touted after winning two world titles in junior series before graduating to compete in the top tier.

Aged 20, he won the championship in his rookie season, and went on to win the title in six of his first seven seasons with Honda, establishing himself as motorcycle racing's dominant force by 2019.

But Marquez suffered a serious crash at the 2020 season-opener in Jerez, broke his arm and endured an extremely rocky road to recovery.

He underwent four operations, was forced to abandon several comeback attempts and was battling with blurred vision, all while his Honda bike was no longer the class of the field, forcing him to push it too hard to try to stay at the front.

Instead of retiring during this bleak spell, something Marquez said he considered, he switched to the smaller Gresini team where he slowly rediscovered his belief and his race-winning pace by ending a drought of more than 3 calendar years with a win in Aragon in 2024.

He then secured a factory weat with Ducati for the 2025 season, and went on to claim a seventh MotoGP title — matching his childhood idol Valentino Rossi's modern-era record.

This season's campaign, culminating in an eighth championship, was arguably unlikelier still. After his early season crash in France, leading to surgery on his shoulder and a foot injury, Marquez returned trailing his championship rivals by 102 points.

But he won six of the subsequent nine races, sealing the championship last weekend in Portimao in Portugal. When he went up to collect his trophy, organizers superimposed a silhouette of a goat (as in "Greatest Of All Time") behind him as he climbed onto the podium.

Marquez himself has however shied away from that title, saying instead that he hoped to be in the discussion as "one of the greatest" in the sport's long history.

entries.title: France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe
entries.summary: A German businessman is accused of supplying equipment to smugglers organizing migrant crossings from France to the United Kingdom. However, he can't face formal charges until he is extradited to France.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

A German businessman is accused of supplying equipment to smugglers organizing migrant crossings from France to the United Kingdom. However, he can't face formal charges until he is extradited to France.

France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.

Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC showed that Marvin R.* of MaRe Boote, managing director of a small firm in western German town Werne, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats smugglers use to journey across the Channel.

According to the media reports, the 35-year-old businessman is accused of supplying smuggling gangs with inflatable boats, engines and life jackets worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

UK authorities estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were responsible for three in every 10 detected crossings during the first four months of this year, the BBC and Le Monde reported.

Arrested and released in Germany

The prosecutor in the northern French city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that "five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country."

According to Finielz, this is part of the investigation about Channel crossings and sinkings since May last year.

The five others are now held in pre-trial detention and were suspected of offenses including "assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others," Finielz told the media.

Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against "the German national implicated in this case," he said, on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.

Marvin R. was arrested and released by German authorities and now required to appear before a French court before January, the prosecutor added.

The BBC wrote that Marvin R. is contesting extradition to France. He can not be formally charged until he is extradited to France, it noted.

How many migrants cross the English Channel?

Migrants frequently cross the English Channel from France to the United Kingdom in small rubber dinghy boats. It is a dangerous journey as the Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year and there have been many deaths.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges us to refrain from revealing the full names.

entries.title: Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
entries.summary: An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.
entries.content:
Europe

Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit

November 27, 2026

An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.

EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.

Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.

There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.

"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.

The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa. 

Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."

Germany demands more for competitiveness, security, defense

Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.

Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."

As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.

In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).

"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."

Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.

"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.

Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.

Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.

They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.

In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.

EU looking elsewhere to raise funds

The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.

The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.

But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.

"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.

Protecting the EU's top triple-A rating

There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.

The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.

EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."

Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.

"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."

EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

entries.title: Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels' most anticipated new art museum, opens its doors
entries.summary: A major addition to Europe's cultural scene: Kanal-Centre Pompidou, the new contemporary art museum in a former Citroen factory complex, is celebrating its opening with a free, nonstop weekend program.
entries.content:
Belgium

Brussels' most anticipated new museum opens its doors

November 27, 2026

A major addition to Europe's cultural scene: Kanal-Centre Pompidou, the new contemporary art museum in a former Citroen factory complex, is celebrating its opening with a free, nonstop weekend program.

Brussels is best known as the de facto capital of the European Union. But beyond its role as a political hub, it also boasts a thriving contemporary art scene.

Yet until now, the Belgian city didn't have a major museum of modern and contemporary art on the scale of Paris' Pompidou or London's Tate Modern. But this will now change with the opening of Kanal-Centre Pompidou on November 28.

The museum aims to "make Brussels a world-class cultural destination," on par with the Guggenheim in Bilbao or the MoMA in New York, Boris Dillies, the head of the regional government, told press agency AFP.

Behind this new museum is an ambitious architectural project involving the transformation of a vast industrial landmark into a multidisciplinary cultural institution.

A modern art museum inside a car factory

Instead of building the new museum from scratch, Kanal was designed to occupy the former Citroen garage and factory complex, built in 1933-34 beside the Brussels canal.

Originally standing as a symbol of modernity and industrial progress, the factory was a space where cars were serviced and assembled, as well as displayed. The former showroom has been transformed into as a glass-and-steel space that rises 21 meters (some 70 feet) high.

Rather than erasing the building's industrial past, the project's architects — noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates, working together as Atelier Kanal — decided to celebrate its original structures. Vast concrete volumes and industrial details remain visible, creating a dialogue between the site's history and its new cultural purpose.

Like London's Tate Modern, which transformed a power station into a museum, Kanal shows how industrial architecture can gain a second life without losing its identity.

"Kanal reveals how architecture can reinvent the museum typology, not only as a place for art, but as a stage for the city and its citizens," Atelier Kanal said in a statement, adding that their concept for the former Citroen factory ensured that the space would be "renewed without being erased, made precise without being overdetermined and open to continued transformation."

Covering around 40,000 square meters (430,550 square feet), the complex is one of the largest cultural buildings in Belgium.

Kanal, Pompidou launch 5-year partnership

Kanal has established a partnership agreement with the Centre Pompidou in Paris that has guided both the international outlook of the new museum, as well as its intention to remain rooted in Brussels' local culture.

"A place for all people" was the founding vision of the Centre Pompidou, articulated by its architects Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano as they designed the iconic institution in the 1970s.

Kanal's collaboration with the Centre Pompidou, which runs until 2031, gives the Brussels museum access to one of the world's greatest collections of modern and contemporary art. Visitors will be able to see works that normally reside in Paris, while also encountering pieces from Belgian collections and newly commissioned projects.

The Brussels museum has already announced some of the upcoming exhibitions that will be drawing from the Pompidou's collection during their five-year partnership: two photography exhibitions focusing on Robert Frank and Brassaï, as well as art exhibitions focusing on iconic figures of modernism: Robert and Sonia Delaunay, Georges Braque, Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse.

The new institution, however, emphasizes that it's not a branch of the Pompidou. The partnership is rather envisioned as a dialogue between two museums with different perspectives and histories.

The Centre Pompidou itself has been closed for major renovations since September 2025, and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.

10 opening exhibitions

The headline exhibition, "A truly immense journey," brings together more than 350 works from the collections of Centre Pompidou, Kanal and numerous Belgian lenders, and will feature modern icons including Lygia Clark, Sonia Delaunay, Alberto Giacometti, Natalia Goncharova, Wifredo Lam and Henri Matisse.

Along with this show, nine other exhibitions fill the building.

One of them, "An infinite woman," focuses on how mass-produced image of a Mangbetu woman long served as a colonial symbol and how artists of African descent have reappropriated and subverted this imagery.

Another one, "Right to the City — Right to the Future," explores the architectural transformation of the Brussels' Quartier Nord, which was historically a working-class neighborhood that was largely cleared in the 1960s to become a high-rise business district — displacing over 15,000 residents.

Museum as a third space

Alongside modern and contemporary art, Kanal is dedicated to architecture, landscape and the performing arts.

This reflects a broader shift in the role of museums, which are increasingly expected to be places where people gather, exchange ideas and engage with contemporary issues rather than simply admire objects behind glass.

The opening program alone demonstrates the museum's ambitions, offering a 36-hour nonstop program of live performances, opening rituals, concerts, DJ sets, films, installations and workshops for children and families, with events open to everyone.

The exhibitions can also be visited for free during the inaugural weekend. Visitors, however, need to have previously booked a time slot; all 30,000 tickets were snapped up within 24 hours of their release.

entries.title: Serbia's Student List runs chemistry professor Radomir Saicic for president
entries.summary: After ousting strongman Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's student movement has now nominated academic Radomir Saicic for the upcoming presidential vote. Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of trying to collapse the state.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia's Student List runs chemistry professor for president

November 27, 2026

After ousting strongman Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's student movement has now nominated academic Radomir Saicic for the upcoming presidential vote. Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of trying to collapse the state.

A long-time supporter of the Serbian student movement, chemistry professor and researcher Radomir Saicic, is set to run for president on behalf of the Student List in late December.

Saicic accepted the nomination on Friday, a day after Serbia's new parliament scheduled the ballot for December 27.

In his acceptance speech, the Belgrade University lecturer said state institutions, including its president, needed to "win back public trust."

"It's time to restore dignity to the office of Serbian president," he said.

"Once we can agree with each other about things that matter to all of us despite our differences, Serbia will have the strength to decide its future on its own, and to have its voice heard and respected in the world," he added.

Vucic barred from running again

The 65-year-old is one of the lawmakers in the new assembly, which was formed in the wake of the Student List ousting the regime of Serbia's longtime strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic at the parliamentary polls last month.

Vucic is banned by the constitution from running for president after winning two terms. He has hinted at his party boycotting the presidential vote.

While the office of the Serbian president is officially far less powerful that the office of Serbian prime minister, Vucic managed to organize his rule around himself during his time as prime minister and then hold on to levers of power while serving as president.

Saicic sees Kosovo as 'occupied territory'

On Friday, Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of "still trying to collapse our state."

"This past decade was marred by the breakdown of the rule of law, corruption, and hate speech," he said.

Saicic, a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Art, is seen by many as a moderate nationalist and a traditionalist.

He has notably described the neigboring, Albanian-dominated Kosovo, as "temporarily occupied territory," keeping in line with Belgrade's long-running policy of treating Kosovo as a breakaway province.

The presidential candidate has also urged a "productive relationship" with Russia, pointing to Serbia's energy needs.

Saicic pledges humility with Bible quote

While seemingly reticent on the topic of the European Union, Saicic told reporters on Friday that he has a "fundamentally positive stance toward Europe and European values," pointing to examples including environment protection, academic education, the rule of law, science and technological progress.

"All of these things we should develop as much as possible, not for the sake of meeting some formal criteria, but to actually be what we are supposed to be," he said.

Saicic has sought to present himself as a devout Orthodox Christian while simultaneously criticizing the Serbian church leaders for aligning with the Vucic regime.

In his Friday speech, Saicic quoted the Bible, saying that "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant."

entries.title: Dutch authorities seize 26 critically endangered turtles from luggage of passenger bound for Hong Kong
entries.summary: The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport. 

The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico. They were only formally discovered and catalogued in 2018 and are one of the smallest of all known species of turtle.

"These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.

How were the turtles discovered and smuggled?

Dutch customs agents discovered the animals on November 21 during a regular inspection and then alerted the NVWA, as the responsible agency for such cases, on realizing that they had uncovered live fauna.

Police then arrested the man at the NVWA's request, and the NVWA said in Friday's statement that he was still in custody, with federal prosecutors continuing their investigations.

"Most of the turtles were packed in a box alongside a toy car, while others were placed inside a sealed sock within a suitcase," the NVWA wrote. "The animals had been wrapped in duct tape, which prevented them from moving. All of the turtles survived the journey."

Authorities said the turtles were being housed at a specialized rescue facility, "where the duct tape was carefully removed," and where they were "receiving the care they require."

What are Vallarta mud turtles?

Vallarta mud turtles are exceptionally small freshwater turtles that only entered the taxonomical record in 2018, endemic to an area in western Mexico.

Relatively little is known about the creature owing both to its recent discovery and the damage to its habitat caused by urbanization and a growing tourist trade in the Mexican state of Jalisco.

The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria — which recently started breeding the turtles in Austria as a "genetic reservoir for eventual rewilding" and is working to help preserve them in Mexico — considers it "the world's smallest turtle species," and estimates that "over 99%" of its natural habitat has been lost to urbanization.

Roads and traffic are a particular risk for the slow-moving creatures.

"Despite strict protections, their small size and striking appearance make them prime targets for illegal collectors," Turtle Island says when detailing other risks to the tiny animals, that are not known to grow larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.

The IUCN Red List classifies it as "Critically Endangered" and it is subject to the highest level of protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). 

"The suspected poaching of 26 of these turtles from the wild may have reduced the population by nearly 10%," the NVWA wrote, basing its figure on the estimated population of around 300 of the turtles in the wild.

The agency urged people to report any suspected instances of illegal trade of protected animal or plant species, whether "via online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets."
